frameworks.name: Solomon Framework
frameworks.definition: A self-advice system in which the founder holds a written back-and-forth dialogue with their imagined 85-year-old self (named Solomon), satisfying the three conditions for trustworthy counsel: aligned incentives, complete context, and competence.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that humans are systematically better at giving advice to others than at following their own advice, a phenomenon he calls the Solomon Paradox (derived from the biblical King Solomon, who gave excellent counsel to other kingdoms while his personal life was in disarray). Because of this asymmetry, reframing self-reflection as giving advice to an imagined future self can yield higher-quality decisions than conventional introspection.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Third-person framing activates the same objective advice-giving process people use when advising others, bypassing the emotional defensiveness that blocks honest self-assessment.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that a trustworthy advisor must satisfy three conditions simultaneously: (1) complete context of the specific situation, (2) competence to evaluate that context, and (3) incentive alignment with the advisee. Any advisor lacking one of the three is structurally unable to give reliable advice regardless of how well they perform on the other two.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
bounded_by: An advisor with context and competence but misaligned incentives (e.g., a therapist paid per recurring session) has structural incentive to prolong, not resolve, the problem.
An advisor with alignment and competence but no context gives generically good but situationally wrong advice.
An advisor with alignment and context but no competence (e.g., a loving but inexperienced parent) cannot convert understanding into actionable guidance.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi identifies professional therapists and executive coaches as structurally misaligned advisors for high-net-worth business operators whose primary problems are operational. The therapist revenue model (recurring session fees) creates a financial incentive to sustain, not resolve, the client's problems.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Client is a business operator facing primarily business-domain problems
Therapist or coach is compensated by recurring session attendance rather than by problem resolution
claims.mechanism: Fee-per-session creates a perverse incentive: problem resolution terminates the revenue stream, so the advisor faces no financial benefit from reaching a conclusion.
bounded_by: Does not apply when the problem domain is psychological rather than operational (e.g., clinical trauma, depression, anxiety).

claims.text: Alex Hormozi reports spending approximately 60 minutes of a typical coaching session merely providing context before an external advisor could offer useful feedback. The Solomon (self-dialogue) framework eliminates this context-loading cost entirely because the self already holds complete situational awareness, allowing sessions to conclude in as little as 7 minutes.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: External advisor has no prior history in the founder's specific situation

numbers.axis: time spent providing context per session before useful feedback is possible

anchors.value: 0 minutes context-loading; can close in as little as 7 minutes, up to 45 minutes for complex issues

claims.text: Alex Hormozi schedules his Solomon self-dialogue in a recurring Monday morning block. The session terminates when the root issue is resolved rather than at a fixed clock time, varying from roughly 7 to 45 minutes depending on issue complexity.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that for high achievers who have already surpassed most peers, comparing performance to contemporaries provides an insufficient motivational standard because they will beat peers regardless. The only motivationally valid comparison target is one's own future self, who has perfect knowledge of how much additional effort was actually available.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Individual has already reached a performance level that regularly surpasses most contemporaries in their domain
claims.mechanism: Peer comparison collapses as a motivational signal once you reliably outperform peers by default; the future-self comparison remains calibrated because that evaluator holds perfect information about residual untapped capacity.
bounded_by: Does not apply to early-stage performers who are not yet ahead of most peers and still need external benchmarks to gauge progress.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that the person one is becoming, not the external outcome achieved, is the primary asset being built by ambitious work. When an outcome fails due to factors outside one's control, the developmental growth embedded in genuine effort is not destroyed and remains the durable return on that investment.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: External outcomes are contingent on factors outside one's control (third-party competence, market conditions); character and capability are accumulated through effort and cannot be reversed by a failed outcome.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that as the financial scale of a business operator's decisions grows, the absolute dollar loss on any single bad bet grows proportionally, and accepting this structural reality is a prerequisite for operating at that scale. Refusing to accept larger losses would require refusing larger bets, which forecloses the upside that only larger bets can produce.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Operator is pursuing large-scale financial outcomes (e.g., targeting $1 billion or more in wealth)
claims.mechanism: Larger bets are the mechanism for larger returns; avoiding the possibility of large losses requires avoiding large bets, which caps upside at the level of small bets.

numbers.axis: bet size and acceptable loss as a function of wealth target

anchors.value: Must accept willingness to lose ~$100M on individual investments

claims.text: Alex Hormozi describes a decision-quality criterion he attributes to Ray Dalio: a missed opportunity should not generate regret if pursuing it would have required applying the same decision process to all comparable opportunities simultaneously, many of which would have produced losses. Correct evaluation is at the portfolio or process level, not the single realized outcome.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Decision quality must be evaluated across the full set of bets made under the same decision process, not at the individual bet level where survivorship bias makes missed winners appear as errors.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi claims that emotional resolution of a problem is the observable signal that a Solomon dialogue session is complete. When an insight closes the mental loop, the issue stops generating cognitive load and the decision or resolution is made. Continuing the session past this point yields no additional benefit.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Mental load from an unresolved issue dissipates when internal dialogue reaches genuine resolution; the felt sense of closure is the measurable endpoint.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that calmness immediately before a high-stakes performance is produced by preparation depth, not by inherent psychological disposition. When a performer has exhausted all available preparation options, no residual improvement action remains and therefore no rational basis for anxiety persists.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Preparation was genuine, comprehensive, and at or near the individual's maximum available effort level
claims.mechanism: Anxiety about performance is driven by uncertainty about whether more preparation would help; exhaustive preparation eliminates that uncertainty, removing the anxiety's rational basis.

numbers.axis: preparation intensity for Hormozi's Leads book presentation

anchors.value: Every day: morning slide review, live recorded run-through, real-time editing while watching recording

examples.text: Alex Hormozi suffered a $15 million loss on a project he had worked on for approximately two years. He had paid several hundred thousand dollars to a vendor whose sole contracted role was to prevent that specific loss. After the loss occurred, he discovered the vendor was simply incompetent rather than malicious. During a subsequent Solomon dialogue session, the insight that closed the loop was: I am the asset you are building. I am satisfied with the effort you put in. And that is enough. Hormozi interpreted this as confirmation that the two years of developmental effort retained its value despite the financial outcome. He compared the experience to a toddler pouring paint on a valuable Babe Ruth Rickey card: the toddler lacks the understanding to be blamed, and the loss simply has to be absorbed.

At the Leads book presentation event, the venue manager told Hormozi she had never seen anyone as calm before an event of that magnitude. Hormozi attributed this to having spent approximately 200 hours over 28 consecutive days in intensive preparation: reviewing slides each morning, recording a live run-through, watching the recording, and editing slides in real time every day. His internal Solomon check confirmed readiness: there was nothing more he could have done to prepare. He noted that even if all cameras had cut off and a storm had disrupted the event, no additional preparation action had been available.

Alex Hormozi cites Ray Dalio's framework for evaluating regret over missed crypto gains. Dalio's position, as Hormozi relays it, was that he did not feel bad about missing early crypto appreciation because if he had applied the same decision logic that would have led him to buy crypto early, he would have had to apply that logic consistently to all comparable uncertain bets, many of which would have destroyed capital. The lesson Hormozi draws is that portfolio-level decision consistency matters more than cherry-picking winning single outcomes in hindsight.

practices.text: Run a weekly Solomon session: at the start of each week (Hormozi uses Monday morning), open a running written document and conduct a back-and-forth dialogue with your imagined 85-year-old self in chat format, continuing until the root issue is resolved. Do not impose a fixed end time; stop when you feel the loop close.

Before engaging any advisor, verify all three conditions: complete contextual knowledge of your specific situation, domain competence matched to your actual problem type, and incentive alignment toward your success rather than toward continued engagement.

When a bad outcome results from a third party's incompetence rather than malice, distinguish clearly between the two in your internal narrative so that emotional response is calibrated to actual agency rather than misattributed blame.
